mediaItem.keyStats:
-   20 wrongfully sentenced to death individuals in Illinois led to the abolishment of the death penalty in the state.
-   Prosecutor Joe Freeman Britt sent 47 people to death row and was in the Guinness Book of World Records as the "deadliest prosecutor".
-   172 people have been exonerated from death row nationwide, including at least nine in North Carolina.
mediaItem.itemTitle: False Confessions Henry McCollum and Leon Brown
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction, False Confessions, hosted by Lauren Nyreider and Steve Trisen, details the wrongful conviction of Henry McCollum and Leon Brown for the rape and murder of 11-year-old Sabrina Bowie in Robison County, North Carolina in 1983.  Both brothers, who had intellectual disabilities, were coerced into false confessions and sentenced to death based largely on these confessions by notorious prosecutor Joe Freeman Britt. Despite evidence pointing to another suspect, Roscoe Artists, and inconsistencies in the confessions, the brothers spent 31 years in prison. DNA evidence in 2014 finally exonerated them, highlighting systemic issues within the justice system, including the dangers of false confessions, prosecutorial misconduct, and the fallibility of the death penalty. The episode underscores the importance of innocence projects and commissions in rectifying wrongful convictions and questions the fairness and accuracy of the death penalty.

featuredIndividual.crimeConvictedOf: Rape and Capital Murder (initially), Rape (upon retrial)
featuredIndividual.sentence: Death Penalty (initially), Life in Prison (upon retrial for rape)
contributingFactorsRaw: False confession (coerced due to severe intellectual disability), implication by brother's false confession, rush to judgment by police, prosecutorial misconduct, ineffective defense.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Center on Wrongful Convictions, North Carolina Innocence Inquiry Commission, AIG Pro Bono program, Paul Weiss Rifkin Morton and Garrison.
innocenceLawyersRaw: Representative Renetta Alston and other lawyers working with Henry McCollum’s case also advocated for Leon. Leon wrote to the North Carolina Innocence Inquiry Commission himself which helped re-open the case.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Yes (exoneree database implied, but not explicitly stated as checked in transcript).
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Same as Henry McCollum - 11-year-old Sabrina Bowie was found dead in a soybean field, raped and suffocated with her own underwear.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Confession obtained after Henry's confession, despite severe intellectual disability and inability to read the confession statement.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Defense attorneys were unable to overcome the confession and the prosecution's case. Judge dismissed murder charges in the second trial, but rape conviction remained.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: DNA testing on a cigarette butt found at the crime scene matched Roscoe Artists, not Henry or Leon. Investigation and re-examination of the case by the North Carolina Innocence Inquiry Commission.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Roscoe Artists (same as Henry McCollum - details listed above).

keyQuotesRaw: "But the way police and prosecutors mishandled this case and condemned two innocent men to death, that's a crime unto itself."
"Henry and Leon are living proof that false confessions can send innocent people to death row."
"People can get so blinded with the horrificness of a crime that moral outrage can distort the search for the truth."

"47 people. I mean, if he weren't a prosecutor, he'd be one of the most prolific serial killers in the United States. 47 people. That's unthinkable." (Regarding Joe Freeman Britt's death penalty record)
Justice Scalia's quote about Sabrina Bowie's case being a justification for the death penalty, contrasted with the brothers' innocence.
Henry McCollum: "It didn't touch my soul...because I didn't kill nobody...God got your judgment right in hell waiting for you."
"No set of rules would be able to guarantee that we only execute the guilty, and only after the guilty receive a fair process." (Justice Blackman on the death penalty)
"Our criminal justice system and our death penalty system, in particular, shouldn't and can't rely on luck to protect innocent people."
systemicIssuesRaw: False confessions, particularly from individuals with intellectual disabilities.
Rush to judgment and tunnel vision in law enforcement investigations under pressure to solve horrific crimes.
Prosecutorial misconduct, including withholding evidence (fingerprint evidence, cigarette butt evidence).
Ineffective defense representation, especially for marginalized individuals against powerful prosecutors.
Flaws and potential for error within the death penalty system.
Racial and socioeconomic disparities within the justice system in Robison County.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Support and expand Innocence Inquiry Commissions like the one in North Carolina in other states.
Reform interrogation practices to prevent false confessions, especially for vulnerable individuals.
Increase scrutiny of prosecutorial conduct and accountability for misconduct.
Improve access to effective legal representation for all defendants, especially those with intellectual disabilities and from marginalized communities.
personalNarrativeRaw: Henry and Leon lost 31 years of their lives to wrongful imprisonment, including time on death row.
The podcast highlights the personal impact of wrongful conviction on Henry and Leon through their brief quotes at the end, showing their resilience and simple joys in freedom.
Henry expresses happiness with his fiancée and simple pleasures like coffee and home-cooked meals.
Leon finds joy in listening to oldies and R&B music and connecting with people in his group home.
The immense psychological toll and trauma of wrongful conviction and death row are implied throughout the narrative, though not explicitly detailed by the exonerees in this episode.
